text: Success Rates of Hair Samples from Brown and American Black Bears

Noninvasively collected hair samples have been used in numerous studies to answer questions about the demographic and genetic status and trends of wildlife populations. In particular, these methods are well-suited for researching and monitoring ursid populations, which are typically difficult to study because of their rare and cryptic nature. Recently, researchers have taken increasing advantage of natural bear behaviors to obtain hair samples for genetic analyses by conducting surveys of bear rubs (objects that bears rub against such as trees and power poles). The low quality and quantity DNA in noninvasively collected samples, however, can result in low genotyping success rates, which may be exacerbated by potentially lengthy duration of environmental exposure. We investigated the effects of environmental exposure (sunlight, moisture, and duration of exposure) on genotyping success rates of brown bear Ursus arctos and American black bear Ursus americanus hair samples. We exposed a total of 238 hair samples from one brown bear and one black bear to multiple treatments for either 30-d or 60-d, periods consistent with collection intervals of recent bear rub survey projects. Sample treatments consisted of full or dappled sunlight, kept dry or saturated with water one to two times daily. We genotyped each sample at three microsatellite loci commonly used in noninvasive genetic studies of bear populations. Our results were consistent with predictions, with all three factors significantly reducing genotyping success rates. Based on our results, we recommend that the specific conditions of field exposure be considered when selecting a suite of microsatellite markers for noninvasive genetic sampling projects, and that researchers carefully consider the duration and environmental conditions that hair samples will be exposed to when designing field studies. Limiting exposure to moisture and sunlight by collecting hairs from bear rubs at relatively short intervals and selecting dry and shaded sites should reduce DNA degradation and thus result in higher genotyping success rates.

Noninvasive genetic sampling methods are commonly used to assess the status and trends of multiple demographic and genetic parameters for many wildlife populations (Waits and Paetkau 2005;Schwartz et al. 2006;Stetz et al. 2011). The suite of noninvasive genetic sampling methods, which includes hair, feces, and urine among others, has increased the scope and efficiency of studies, particularly those of cryptic species such as mountain lions Puma concolor (Sawaya et al. 2011) and wolverine Gulo gulo (Flagstad et al. 2004), that often inhabit remote, rugged landscapes where live-trapping of animals presents substantial challenges. The noninvasive nature of sample collection is also advantageous when working with vulnerable populations, and can often be adapted to citizen science programs.
Sequences of DNA, such as those targeted by microsatellite primers, can be easily broken because DNA is a fragile molecule (Lindahl 1993). Environmental exposure, primarily moisture and ultraviolet radiation, along with collection and storage methods, can degrade DNA in biological samples, with cool, dry conditions expected to minimize degradation (Hofreiter et al. 2001;Roon et al. 2003). Although several studies have evaluated the role of environmental exposure on DNA degradation in fecal samples (e.g., Piggott 2004;Murphy et al. 2007;Demay et al. 2013), to our knowledge no such research has been published for hair samples. Understanding the effects of exposure on DNA degradation in noninvasively collected hair samples is an important component for study design in order to minimize the loss of animal detections due to failed genotyping. Missed detection events of individual animals can contribute to numerous problems, such as adding to capture probability heterogeneity that can bias markrecapture parameter estimates like abundance and population growth rates (Mills et al. 2000). If detections are missed at a large enough scale or are systematic in nature, measures of genetic population structure may also be biased (Landguth et al. 2012).
Perhaps more than any other taxa, noninvasive genetic sampling methods have been used for monitoring brown Ursus arctos and American black bear Ursus americanus populations, most often by collecting hair samples from baited, barbed-wire hair traps deployed systematically and surveyed at 10-14-d intervals (e.g., Woods et al. 1999;Kendall et al. 2008;Sawaya et al. 2012;van Manen et al. 2012). Increasingly, however, researchers are obtaining hair samples by exploiting bears' natural behavior of rubbing on trees, power poles, and similar objects (hereafter, ''bear rubs''; Karamanlidis et al. 2007;Kendall et al. 2009;Stetz et al. 2010;Latham et al. 2012;Sawaya et al. 2012). Although this behavior is not well-understood, it is believed to be nearly ubiquitous across the ranges of brown and black bears (Burst and Pelton 1983;Green and Mattson 2003;Karamanlidis et al. 2007;Latham et al. 2012), and it provides a safe, efficient means to genetically sample a potentially large proportion of a population. Relative to hair traps, bear rub surveys are often conducted at longer and more variable intervals, ranging from days to months (Stetz et al. 2010).
As with any noninvasive genetic sampling approach, concerns about the quantity and quality of DNA exist with bear rub hair samples, in part due to the potentially lengthy exposure to sunlight and moisture, which are factors known to degrade DNA (Pompanon et al. 2005;Thacker et al. 2006). We designed a study to imitate field conditions typical of bear rub surveys in temperate, forested areas to evaluate the effects that environmental exposure had on genotyping success rates of bear hair samples. To test our hypothesis that moisture, sunlight, and duration of exposure affect genotyping success, we subjected 238 hair samples to different levels of sunlight and moisture for either 30 or 60 d, after which we analyzed three microsatellite loci per sample. We predicted that genotyping success rates would decline with increased moisture, ultraviolet radiation, and duration of exposure.

As part of routine live-trapping efforts, we obtained a large number of hairs from one brown and one black bear in northwestern Montana. The adult male brown bear was captured in the Blackfoot River drainage east of Missoula, Montana; the adult female black bear was captured in Mesler Creek north of Libby, Montana. Handling and immobilization procedures followed the Montana Animal Care and Use Committee protocols for brown bears and black bears (Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks 2004). To minimize degradation, we immediately placed hairs on silica desiccating beads in cool, dark conditions until treatments began approximately 1 mo later. Under these conditions, we expected negligible loss of target DNA (Roon et al. 2003).
We affixed clusters of hairs of approximately the same size as those collected from bear rubs (approx. 15 hairs) to untreated pine boards, which we then surrounded with chicken wire to minimize loss of hairs to physical disturbance. We established one board for each treatment, which included both species and both durations of exposure (i.e., 30 or 60 d). Our treatments consisted of all combinations of full and shaded (dappled) sunlight, either kept dry or saturated with water one or two times daily (Table 1), for either 30 or 60 d. We placed the full sunlight treatment to receive maximum solar radiation in order to replicate open-country bear rubs, such as telephone poles, which often receive little or no shade. Most bear rubs, however, are found on forest trails, which provide at least partial shade. We therefore placed the shaded treatment beneath the canopy of a mature Engelmann spruce Picea engelmannii tree. The dry treatment received no special efforts because there is typically little precipitation during this season where the experiment was conducted (Missoula, Montana). We used an automatic sprinkler to gently saturate samples with water one or two times per day, for 5 min each, for the final treatment to reflect weather typical of intermountain areas.
To assess the differences between treatment factors, we used HOBO data-loggers (Model U12-012; Onset Computer Corporation, Bourne, Massachusetts) to record

We selected three nuclear microsatellite loci that have been used in the majority of published brown and black bear noninvasive genetic sampling studies (G10J, G10P, and G10M; Paetkau et al. 1995). These loci have allele lengths common to many bear studies, ranging from 157 base-pairs (bp) to 218 bp (G10P and G10M, respectively). We used a direct-to-PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) technique (McCusker et al. 1992) that started with clipping one guard hair root into a tube of PCR mix, bypassing DNA purification. We ran the multiplex at 60uC for 40 cycles.
To minimize variation due to reagents, equipment, or experimental technique, we created a single PCR master mix sufficient for all amplifications (240 anticipated study samples plus 16 positive controls). The mix contained 50 mM KCl, 0.1% Trition X-100, and 160 mM dNTPs in a volume of 15 mL following Paetkau et al. (1998). We froze the mix in four equal aliquots, each sufficient for 64 PCR reactions, which is the approximate number that can be processed through our sequencer in 24 h, and a manageable number of hair follicles to clip into PCR mixes in a single sitting by one technician. We eliminated variation between lasers, processors, polymer, or other variables that impact sequencer optics by using the same thermocycler, sequencer, and capillary for all amplifications. All genetic analyses were conducted at a lab specializing in low-quality samples (Wildlife Genetics International, Nelson, British Columbia).
To reduce the rate of failed results for homozygous genotypes, we established a single peak-height threshold of 300 relative florescence units for high-confidence scoring. We scored each locus as one of the following: HC (high confidence, accurate genotype that meets the strength threshold), Failed (does not meet strength threshold or is not scored as a high confidence result by two experienced technicians; Paetkau 2003), FA (false amplification of an allele above the strength threshold), or ADO (allelic dropout where the amplified allele did not meet the strength threshold).

We first tested for normality of each treatment factor using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test. We then used an Ftest for the assumption of equal variances on those factors that followed a normal distribution. Finally, we used a 2-sample t-test assuming equal variances to test for significant differences between each treatment for each factor.
We used mixed-effects logistic regression to model the relationship between multilocus genotype success and treatment factors (moisture, sunlight, and duration of exposure). Categorical fixed effects included duration of exposure (30 or 60 d), light intensity (partially shaded or full sunlight), and moisture (dry or saturated daily). We used species (black or brown bear) as a random effect. For both sets of models we explored single factors as well as additive and interaction effects. Support for models was determined based on Akaike Information Criterion correct for small sample size (AIC c ) values (Burnham and Anderson 2002). All analyses were conducted in the R statistical software (R Development Core Team 2006). Our annotated code can be found in Text S1 (Supplemental Material).

For the shaded treatment, temperature during the study ranged from 23uC to 44uC, with a daily average minimum and maximum temperature of 8uC and 26uC, respectively (Data S2, Supplemental Material). Maximum relative humidity ranged from 47% to 97%, with a daily average maximum of 73%. For the full sunlight treatment, temperature ranged from 28uC to 59uC, with a daily average minimum and maximum temperature of 5uC and 37uC, respectively. Maximum relative humidity ranged from 45% to 100%, with a daily average of 77%. Light intensity exceeded the range of the data-logger 92% and 18% of the days in the full sun and dappled sun treatments, respectively. As such, we were unable to statistically test for differences in ultraviolet radiation levels.
Excluding light intensity, all other factors met the assumption of normality and of equal variances. There was a significant difference between maximum temperature (P , 0.0001) and maximum humidity (P = 0.0366) across treatments. Average temperature, however, was not significantly different between treatments (P = 0.24123), likely due to similar nighttime temperatures.
Beyond the difference in maximum humidity, our design saturated the ''moisture'' treatment samples one or two times per day, whereas the dry treatment was exposed to only a single precipitation event during the entire course of our experiment.

All control samples (n = 16), which were not exposed to sunlight or moisture, produced high-quality genotypes for all three loci. Across experimental treatments, only one sample exhibited allelic dropout and only six (2%) samples exhibited false alleles after 30 d (Table Data S3, Supplemental Material). This rate changed little after 60 d, with just one sample exhibiting allelic dropout and 10 (3%) samples exhibiting false alleles. Seventeen of these 18 (94%) errors occurred with the G10P locus, which had the shortest allele lengths of the three loci. Genotype failure (as determined by inadequate peak strength) occurred across all loci. Notably, G10M, the locus with the longest alleles, exhibited the highest failure rate after both 30 and 60 d (37% and 86%, respectively). The G10J locus had the highest amplification success rate after 60 d (29%), despite being of intermediate length between G10P and G10M (Table 2). We observed reductions in single-locus genotyping success rates as moisture, ultraviolet radiation, and duration of exposure increased (Figure 1).
Based on AIC c values, our mixed-effects logistic regression model with additive effects of duration of exposure, full sunlight, and moisture on genotyping success had the greatest support in our data, with 95% of the AIC c weight (Table 3). The only other model to receive any support in our data included effects of full sunlight and moisture (AIC c weight = 5%); however, support was low (DAIC c = 5.69). Each treatment factor had significant negative effects (P , 0.01) on genotyping success (Table 4).

Our results demonstrated that exposure of bear hair to moisture or ultraviolet radiation for 30 or 60 d significantly reduced microsatellite genotyping success relative to control samples. These results emphasize the need to consider environmental exposure in the design of noninvasive genetic sampling studies, particularly those using bear rubs to obtain hair samples, the logistical flexibility of which is well-suited for large-scale, long-term projects estimating parameters such as population growth rate and genetic population structure (Karamanlidis et al. 2007;Stetz et al. 2010;Sawaya et al. 2012). A better understanding of the decline in genotyping success as a function of exposure to the environment will serve to improve study design by minimizing the loss of detection events, which can bias estimates through introducing heterogeneity in detection probabilities or outright omitting individuals from the analysis.
Numerous similar experiments have been conducted with feces in ursids and other taxa (e.g., Murphy et al. 2003;Piggott 2004;Panasci et al. 2011;Demay et al. 2013). As a result of considerably greater quality-control issues, genotyping feces for bears remains an economically infeasible option for many studies. Conversely, hair collection methods have seen widespread success, with the trend of moving from systematically distributed, baited sites to repeated surveys of bear rubs (Stetz et al. 2010;Sawaya et al. 2012).

Consistent with our predictions, amplification success was significantly lower in samples exposed to moisture daily, samples exposed to full sunlight, and samples exposed to the environment for 60 d relative to samples kept dry, shaded, and exposed to the environment for 30 d, respectively (Tables 3,4). Regardless of the duration of exposure, we observed the highest genotyping success rates in hairs kept dry and shaded, which minimized the two factors believed to be responsible for most DNA degradation in noninvasively collected hair samples.
We found a significant decline in amplification success in samples that were exposed to moisture daily relative to samples that were kept dry. This result is similar to that of Piggott (2004), who hypothesized that increased rainfall in winter resulted in lower amplification rates in brush-tailed rock-wallaby Petrogale penicillata and red fox Vulpes vulpes fecal samples, although they did not test this explicitly. Interestingly, we observed a potential rescue effect of full sunlight on wet samples relative to shaded wet samples (Figure 1). This could be explained by the fact that samples exposed to full sunlight dried more rapidly, reducing the degrading effect of moisture. This interaction was somewhat masked, however, by the near complete failure of black bear hairs in the 60-d exposure treatment, the cause of which is unknown.
We hypothesized that increased exposure of hairs to ultraviolet radiation would degrade the DNA within them, resulting in increased amplification failures relative to samples kept in the shade. It is possible, however, that the significantly higher temperatures that our full-sun samples experienced was at least partially responsible for the increased failure rate that we observed. For example, Nsubuga et al. (2004) investigated the effect of multiple factors on DNA concentration in gorilla Gorilla beringei beringei feces, including age of sample and weather. Although their top model explained only a small amount of the variation, they found that DNA concentration decreased significantly with increasing temperature at the time of collection (Nsubuga et al. 2004). Future research on the drivers of DNA degradation in the field should attempt to tease apart the effects of temperature and ultraviolet radiation.
Although we were not able to formally model false allele and allelic dropout rates, our results are consistent with those of similar studies that found increasing rates of genotyping errors and failures as fecal samples aged (e.g., Lucchini et al. 2002;Piggott 2004;Santini et al. 2007). In a study on pygmy rabbit Brachylagus idahoensis fecal samples, Demay et al. (2013)   with scat analyses than with hair, such as diet and soil conditions; however, both sample types clearly exhibit a negative relationship between the duration of environmental exposure and amplification success.
Longer alleles have been found to have lower amplification success rates in similar experiments with noninvasively collected samples. Demay et al. (2013) found the lowest success (39.6-41.5%) for the longest alleles (188-221 bp), compared with 48% success for the shortest alleles (111-134 bp) for pygmy rabbit fecal samples. Our allele lengths ranged from 157 to 218 bp, similar to the longest alleles of Demay et al. (2013), but well within the range typical of microsatellites used in most bear noninvasive genetic sampling studies. We intended to model false allele and allelic dropout rates as well; however, because of the low rate of occurrences, we could not perform these analyses. Further, it was possible that nonspecific (i.e., false) peaks from G10M may have confounded scoring of G10P alleles, because these may have been difficult to distinguish, even by experienced technicians. Finally, with two of six singlelocus genotypes being homozygous (G10J 190.190; G10P 157.157), there were few opportunities for allelic dropout to occur.
Our results demonstrated a decline in DNA amplification rates, and thus genotyping success rates, for hair samples in environments typical of many intermountain bear populations, and have implications for noninvasive genetic sampling studies of any number of wildlife species. Regardless of sample type, we recommend that researchers consider the effects of degradation on genotyping success rates when designing noninvasive genetic sampling-based field studies in order to minimize downstream impacts to population parameter estimation. We also encourage additional controlled experiments to provide greater insights into the causes and rates of DNA degradation, and to develop means to mitigate their effects, such as sampling-site selection and more rigorous DNA purification. Researchers must determine the optimal balance between logistical considerations of survey intervals with the potential loss of detection events due to DNA degradation in the field, and should identify ways to minimize exposure whenever possible, such as placing sites in more shaded areas and shielding hairs from rain. Finally, we suggest that pilot studies be conducted to inform the selection of genetic markers, using samples similar to those that will be collected in the field, and including factors such as moisture, ultraviolet radiation, and the duration of exposure prior to collection (Taberlet et al. 1999;Piggott 2004).

Molecular sex identification of red panda (Ailurus fulgens) suitable for noninvasive genetic studies

Molecular sexing of wild animals is feasible with differential amplification of X-and Y-homologous regions of various genes. We present a simple and robust technique for sex identification of red panda suitable for noninvasive studies based on sex-specific fragment size polymorphism in amelogenin (AMEL) gene. Sequence analysis of AMELX and AMELY revealed an 18-bp deletion in Y fragment which was used to differentially amplify 217 bp of X and 199 bp of Y fragments. The designed primer pair is very sensitive and exhibits polymerase chain reaction (PCR) success rates of 89 and 78 % at 0.1 and 0.01 ng template DNA concentrations, respectively. Further, we amplified poor quality faecal DNA with 94 % success rate and average dropout rate of 15.6 %. In silico analysis shows that these primers can also be used to identify sex of a sympatric species, giant panda.

Noninvasive genetics has led to remarkable changes in population studies of endangered species (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). This approach is especially useful in generating large-scale molecular data on elusive species without handling or even seeing them, from shed samples like hair, skin, feathers and faeces (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009;Reddy et al. 2012). Major challenges of working with such samples are low quality and quantity of DNA, genotyping errors and low amplification success rates (Taberlet et al. 1996). These issues are effectively addressed in studies which identify and quantify target DNA (Morin et al. 2001), use multi-tube method (Taberlet et al. 1996) and use multiplex DNA amplification (Arandjelovic et al. 2009), making noninvasive DNA analysis a robust method for assessing population parameters of wild animals.
Sex identification and sex ratio assessment provide crucial data on population dynamics of wild animals (Xu et al. 2010). Sex can be assessed by karyotyping, presence of Y-antigen, Xlinked enzymes and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), of which PCR is a reliable, accurate and sensitive technique (Fernández Feijóo et al. 2010). PCR-based identification can be achieved by amplifying Y-specific SRY gene (Woods et al. 1999); however, an amplification failure can result in a false inference of a male as a female (Bidon et al. 2013). Internal mitochondrial controls can be used to address this problem (Kamimura et al. 1997), but there exists an inherent risk of preferential amplification, as mitochondrial sequences occur in higher copy numbers than Y-chromosome sequences (Durnin et al. 2006). Therefore, the most preferred technique is differential amplification of alleles located on homologous regions of sex chromosomes (Xu et al. 2010), such as zinc finger locus (ZnF) and amelogenin gene (AMEL) (Pilgrim et al. 2005). Length polymorphisms in AMEL and ZnF have been used in molecular sexing of free ranging animals like Communicated by M. Japanese black bear (Ursus thibetanus japonicus) (Yamamoto et al. 2002), felids (Pilgrim et al. 2005), giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) (Xu et al. 2007(Xu et al. , 2010) ) and ursids (Pagès et al. 2008). Amplification-refractory mutation system (ARMS) is also used to differentially amplify X-and Ychromosomal regions (Li et al. 2011).
Red panda (Ailurus fulgens) is a specialized carnivore that primarily feeds on bamboo and is distributed widely in the Himalaya and Hengduan mountains (Li et al. 2005;Hu et al. 2011;Wei et al. 2015). This endangered species is extremely difficult to monitor in the wild because of its elusive, wary and nocturnal behavior (Hodgson et al. 1847;Johnson et al. 1988;Holst 1989;Stevenson et al. 1989;Guo et al. 2011). Red panda is sympatric to giant panda, another important conservation flagship species, across large parts of its range. Despite being an important species, information on red panda from India is scanty mainly due to difficulty in studying this elusive and solitary animal, which dwells in mountainous ranges with dense forest cover. In addition to determining occupancy and population numbers of red panda, it is also crucial to determine sex ratio to understand its population dynamics, dispersal patterns and behavior (Durnin et al. 2006).
Here, we describe a simple and robust molecular sexing method based on sex-specific length polymorphism of amelogenin (AMEL) gene in red panda. We also test the efficiency of our primers for amplification at picogram concentrations of template DNA suitable for noninvasively collected samples.

Fresh faecal samples were collected from 15 red pandas housed at Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park, Darjeeling, in sterile bottles with 90 % ethanol. Blood samples of seven red pandas were collected in EDTA-coated vacutainer tubes. All samples were transported to the laboratory within a month and stored at -20 °C until extraction. DNA was isolated from blood by phenol-chloroform method (Sambrook et al. 1989) and from outer layer of faecal samples with QIAamp DNA stool mini kit (Qiagen).

Exon-5 of amelogenin gene of red panda was partially amplified as described by Yamamoto et al. (2002). AMELX fragment from females and AMELX and AMELY fragments from males were run on agarose gel, purified using QIAquick gel extraction kit (Qiagen) and sequenced by Big dye terminator cycle sequencing in ABI 3730 DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). Sequences were analysed and edited with CodonCode Aligner v4.2 (GenBank accession numbers-KM017653 for AMELX and KM017654 for AMELY). These sequences were aligned and analysed for sequence polymorphism with MEGA v5.0 (Tamura et al. 2011) and ClustalW2 Online tool from EBI (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/msa/ clustalw2/). Internal primer pair (RP-AmlF 5′-ACACTCCA TGACTCCAACCC-3′ and RP-AmlR 5′-CTGTATGGGGAA CATCGGAG-3′) was designed flanking the polymorphic region in AMELX and AMELY with Primer3 Plus (Untergasser et al. 2007) and was used to amplify 199 and 217 bp of AMELY and AMELX, respectively, with the following PCR conditions: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 20 s, 54 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 30 s, and final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. PCR reaction mixture (15 μl) included 10 ng of template DNA, 1X Ex-Taq Buffer (Takara), 200 μM of each dNTP, 1.5 μg of BSA, 1.5 μM each of forward and reverse primer and 1 U of Ex-Taq polymerase (Takara). Since red panda is a specialized carnivore which feeds mainly on bamboo, contamination of faecal DNA with prey DNA is uncertain or possibly insignificant. However, as giant panda is often seen in sympatry with red panda, our primers were also tested for in silico PCR (Yu and Zhang 2011) of partial amelogenin sequences of giant panda (GenBank accession numbers EF635972, EF635973).  Blood genomic DNA of six red pandas males and three females) was serially diluted at 1:10 ratio from 10 to 0.001 ng/μl concentration and amplified with labeled RP-Aml primers in triplicates. In addition to agarose gel electrophoresis, PCR products were also electrophoresed in ABI 3730 DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems) with an internal LIZ size standard (Applied Biosystems). Alleles were scored with GeneMapper v3.2 software. Primers were finally tested for their ability to amplify DNA from faecal samples of 15 captive red pandas (ten males and five females).

We describe a PCR method suitable for DNA-based sex identification of red panda from poor quality samples like faeces. Only one paper so far describes sex identification of red panda using ARMS PCR to detect sequence differences in X-and Yhomologous regions of zinc finger locus (ZnF) (Li et al. 2011). However, ARMS technique suffers an innate risk of preferential amplification of one amplicon over the other and is not suitable for molecular sexing (Xu et al. 2010). It is also our personal experience that ARMS technique requires pure genomic DNA like that obtained from blood and tissue, and is not suitable for noninvasive samples like faeces (present study, data not shown) and feathers (Reddy et al. 2007). It is simpler to use a single primer pair to detect length polymorphisms in X-and Yhomologous loci. Further, contrary to findings by Li et al. (2011), we obtained length polymorphism in homologous sequences of amelogenin (AMEL) gene in red panda (Fig. S1).
Approximately 430 bp of AMELX and 410 bp of AMELY were amplified and sequenced in red panda using the primers described by Yamamoto et al. (2002). Sequence alignment showed 18 and 63-bp deletions in AMELY of red panda and giant panda respectively (Fig. S1). Based on the length polymorphism between homologous amplicons, a new primer pair (RP-AmlF and RP-AmlR) was designed to amplify 217 and 199 bp of AMELX and AMELY, respectively, in red panda samples. Male samples produced amplicons of two sizes (199 and 217 bp), while female samples produced a single amplicon of 217 bp (Fig. 1a,b). The same primer pair, when tested in silico, amplified 214 and 151 bp of AMELX and AMELY, respectively, in giant panda (Fig. S1). This is advantageous as short PCR fragments (<250 bp) facilitate analysis of degraded DNA (Bidon et al. 2013). The diagnostic AMELY amplicon is smaller than AMELX amplicon, thereby avoiding misclassification of low quality male samples as females, as longer amplicons are more prone to amplification failure (Bidon et al. 2013). Size difference of 18 bp between AMELX and AMELY amplicons can be clearly resolved on 2.5 % agarose gel. However, in case of degraded DNA, amplicon sizes can also be determined by automated capillary electrophoresis.
Our primer pair is sensitive and could amplify template DNA concentrations of 0.1 ng with 89 % success and 0.01 ng with 78 % success when tested on blood samples (Table 1, Fig. S2). Dropout rate was higher for AMELX than the diagnostic AMELY amplicon, thereby confirming preferential amplification of the smaller Y fragment than the larger homologous X fragment. Dropout rate was also used to calculate the number of repetitions needed to obtain results with 99.99 % certainty for the homozygous (female) samples (Table 1). Sensitivity of these primers on low quality faecal DNA from 15 red pandas was good (Fig. S3), and we obtained 94.2 % PCR success with 15.6 % dropout rate in ten heterozygous (male) samples. Four PCR replications were needed to obtain results with 99.99 % certainty with faecal DNA samples.
Our newly developed PCR protocol was successfully applied to the captive red panda population in Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park, and will facilitate sex identification of newborn animals in captivity. This technique can also be used to establish sex ratio of wild populations through analysis of noninvasive samples.
